Year-Forth:
"In 1907, Max Jacob lived at the end of a courtyard, in a kind of shed tucked in between two buildings, which looked straight out on to dustbins. The place was tiny (like all of his lodgings) and very dark. It looked like a storage space that had been emptied of its rubbish and brooms and rented out at a hundred francs a year. It was an accurate reflection, in any case, of the poet's extreme poverty. He wrote with a pen that cost two sous, ate rice pudding, borrowed fifty centimes to take the tram, tightened his belt so he could repay his debts as soon as possible, and spent the greater part of his meagre earnings on fuel for the oil lamp, which burned night and day since the single room was so dark ... He cleaned the place carefully. The room was furnished with a mattress placed on four bricks, a table, a chair, and a trunk in which the poet kept his manuscripts. After much insistence, he had managed to get the owner to make an opening in the zinc of the roof to put a skylight there. On the largest wall, in chalk, he had drawn the signs of the zodiac, an image of Christ, a self-portrait painted at a time when he had had a beard, and various inscriptions, one of which immediately struck the eye: 'Never go to Montparnasse.' Max received clients on Mondays. He was very courteous to his visitors, welcoming them himself and asking them to have a seat in a corner of the room, where several inhabitants of the neighborhood were already waiting. Then he would go back to telling the fortune of the person he had been with when interrupted. [He had made a name for himself as an astrologer]" (cf. Franck 2001, 37).

Soon after moving to Paris, Amedeo Modigliani meets the doctor Paul Alexandre, who is his first patron, as well as being one of his first suppliers of hashish. The doctor had rented a house on the rue du Delta, where he welcomes poor artists, including Gleizes, Le Fauconnier, the sculptor Drouard and Brancusi. Modigliani exhibits his paintings there. Paul Alexandre would pose for him and buy a great number of his works. He would persuade him to exhibit at the Salon des Indépendants. Apollinaire would help him sell his paintings. Paul Guillaume, who would be his first dealer, would be introduced to him by another friend, Max Jacob (cf. Franck 2001, 189).

Mme. Cocteau leaves the house in Rue La Bruyère and moves to a smaller home at 62 Rue Malakoff (now called Avenue Raymond-Poincaré) where she is able to maintain the lifestyle to which she is accustomed. Henceforth she lives alone with Cocteau. Cocteau begins to attend the Académie Royale de Beaux-Arts and l’École des Arts Decoratifs.

After a brief stint as a reporter for The Evening Post in New York, Walter Arensberg returns to Boston and marries Mary Louise Stevens whose family had emigrated from Dresden in the early 1880s.

Albert C. Barnes buys out his partner Hermann Hille, and becomes a millionaire at the age of 35.

Gottlieb Friedrich von Reber (1880-1959) marries Erna Sander, from a wealthy family, allowing him to leave his job and concentrate on art collecting (cf. Geelhar 1993, 157-158).

La Brasserie-Cinéma Rochechouart's importance as a cinema venue emerges between 1907 and 1908 (66, Rue de Rochechouart). The "cinéma-brasserie" and the "bar-cinéma" are evocative early spaces where Salmon, Picasso, Jacob, and Apollinaire may have had amusing misadventures consuming food, alcohol, absinthe, and social banter, as well as the cinema. These spaces imply the extent to which the cinema is consumed as simply another disorienting "course" of entertainment among many. Because some brasserie- or bar-cinémas only sporadically use films as an attractive lure, and also often suddenly cease to project films when public ordinances seek a tighter control of film exhibition, many of these spaces are often never archived within public record (cf. Wild 2007, 160).

By this time Delaunay has met Léger and Le Fauconnier (cf. Golding 1968, 23).

Brancusi moves to a new studio at 54, rue du Montparnasse (cf. Ernoult & Lassale 2019, 164).
Late-January:
Through EARLY-FEBRUARY, Derain makes the third trip to London.
January: Documents
Around this time or by FEBRUARY, picks up Marie Laurencin at Sagot's gallery. He decides that she would be a great companion for Apollinaire (cf. Richardson 1996, 63). (Others date Picasso's encounter with her to SPRING - cf. Roe 2015, 183).

"Fernande Olivier described her as having the face of a goat, short-sighted eyes, a pointy nose, skin the color of dirty ivory, long, red hands, and something of the perverse little girl about her. Not to mention that she was affected, liked to listen to herself talk, and played the ingénue. Fernande hated her, probably because, in this group in which there were not many women, Marie Laurencin was her greatest potential rival for first place" (cf. Franck 2001, 82).

The minister of the interior Georges Clemenceau surprisingly appoints the police officer Célestin Hennion as the head of the Sureté Générale. Hennion is tasked with creating the intelligence agency that would monitor foreigners (cf. Cohen-Solal 2023, 132).
Early-Year: Documents Item Commentary
When the Steins realize the problem Picasso is having finding a place to concentrate on his work, they come to the rescue and agree to pay the rent for another studio on another floor of the Bateau-Lavoir, No. 13, rue Ravignan in Paris (cf. Richardson 1991, 474).

At some point Lola writes to him at No. 13, rue Ravignan (cf. Gual 2021, 76).

'Nudes' continue to be dominant subject in Picasso's work as in the ink drawings Nu debout [OPP.07:395], Nu de profil marchant [OPP.07:397], Femme debout de dos [OPP.07:403] and Nu feminin allongé [OPP.07:390] (cf. Fluegel 1980, 86). Partially spurred on by Matisse's Bonheur de vivre, Picasso begins sketches intended for a monumental figure composition of sailors going to a bordello. Among them are the oil on canvas Les demoiselles d'Avignon (Étude) [OPP.07:371]; and the pastel Les demoiselles d'Avignon (Étude) [OPP.07:022].

Richardson sees a connection between drawings of carriages in the Bois de Boulogne - cf. Étude pour des cavaliers au Bois de Boulogne: femme debout [OPP.07:006], Personnages et chevaux [OPP.07:670] - and these first sketches of a a whorehouse. In an article by Baudelaire on Constantin Guys entitled "Le Peintre de la vie moderne", he postulates that two of the quintessentially "modern" subjects for an artist to address are the brothel and the procession of carriage folk in the Bois. According to Baudelaire, the whore is "a perfect image of savagery in the midst of civilization" (cf. Richardson 1996, 13-14).

Also makes the gouache Portrait de Max Jacob [OPP.07:005]; and the sarcastic drawing in black crayon Bon jour Mlle. Cone (Autoportrait) [OPP.07:470].

"He was perfectly open about the continuing influence of the Catalan Romanesque sculpture and frescoes he had known in his youth, just as considerably later he acknowledged the importance of Iberian art to his painting at this period ... Picasso was aware of African, Oceanic, and other 'primitive' carvings, but not yet acutely aware of them" (cf. O'Brian 1994, 148-149).

"The Steins' Saturday-night soirées were crowded with artists, dealers and bohemian hangers-on. The house at 27, rue de Fleurus was becoming a sort of sparring ground where artists could confront and debate with one another. It was also a place where they could see new work at a time when reproductions were rare and only in black and white - and paintings that had scandalized the public. Matisse had just shown Blue Nude at the Salon des Indépendants, where Leo Stein had quickly snapped it up. When Sarah Stein saw it, she decided she would from now on collect nothing but Matisse. She had already acquired over fifty of his works; she visited him nearly every week and would spend the rest of the year going through her collection, replacing other artists' work with his and in the process wresting a dozen recent works from Leo and Gertrude" (cf. Roe 2015, 176).

"The house [at 27, rue de Fleurus] had two stories, and an adjoining workshop. On the house side, there were a few rooms, a bathroom, a kitchen big enough to eat dinner in. The studio side consisted of an enormous room, which contained polished Italian Renaissance furniture, a stove, two or three tables bearing flowers and porcelain, a fireplace, a massive cross hung between two windows, and had whitewashed walls without an inch of bare space left on them. They were completely covered with the works of Gauguin, Delacroix, El Greco, Manet, Braque, Vallotton, Cézanne, Renoir, Matisse, Picasso, and others" (cf. Franck 2001, 90).

Kahnweiler informs his family that he is interested in a career as an art merchant. They send him to the dealer Wertheimer, specializing in 18th century painting. Kahnweiler explains to him that he is more interested in contemporary art. His uncle gives him a 1,000 GBP loan to purchase art and open a gallery. Kahnweiler exchanges numerous letters with his friend Eugène Reignier, looking for advice (cf. Monod-Fontaine 1994, 42). (Others claim that he receives 25,000 GFR (gold francs) - cf. Franck 2001, 153).
January 1:
Eyre Crowe's (British Foreign Office) memorandum on English interest in preserving balance of power and joining 2nd most powerful country in Europe (France); comments on German foreign policy and confrontation possible.
Early-January:
The sculpture Reclining Nude (I) is damaged in modeling; Matisse paints the same motif as Blue Nude: Memory of Biskra, and completes the sculpture afterward (cf. Cousins & Elderfield 1992, 135).

At 62, bis rue de Douai, the Artistic Cinéma Pathé opens in what had been formerly a convent for the zealous Dames de la Sainte-Euchariste; the cinema would be later renovated in 1913 and relocated one door down from the former address (61, rue de Douai) where 496 spectators could be seated. As indicated in the 1908 Artistic Cinéma film program, Picasso and Salmon may have seen a typically mixed film program punctuated by orchestral entr'actes. The program archetypically interweaves various actualités and travel views depicting Tunisian and artesian woodworkers (Petits métiers tunistens; Artiste tourneur sur bois), winter sports (Les Sports d'hiver à Chamonix), or a bull fight in Seville (Course de Taureaux à Seville) with comedies (Apaches mal avisés and Boireau fait la Noce, both of which starred the comedian André Deed), dramas (La Belle et la Bete), and what may have been Segundo de Chamón's fantastical Red Specter of 1907 (Le Spectre) (cf. Wild 2007, 159).
January 25:
Reichstag elections.

Febuary:
Braque, who had spent the WINTER months in L'Estanque also returns to Paris. He has involuntarily grown away from Matisse (cf. Cousins & Daix 1989, 342; Richardson 1996, 68). (Others date his trip to MARCH - cf. Roe 2015, 178).

Through MARCH, exhibition of Islamic textiles and miniatures at the Musée des Arts Décoratifs (Pavillon de Marsan) (cf. Cousins & Elderfield 1992, 136).

Félix Fénéon, now acquiring new work for the Bernheim-Jeunes, writes to Matisse offering him a one-man show. Soon afterwards, he visits the artist in his studio, where he buys three paintings and makes him a proposal: the Bernheim-Jeunes are offering to purchase the bulk of all his future work in return for first refusal. With the Steins as competitors, the Bernheim-Jeunes would soon be setting prices for Matisse's work at thousands rather than hundreds of francs (cf. Roe 2015, 176).

Léon Delagrange, a sculptor who had known Gabriel Voisin at the Beaux-Arts, has a real passion for aviation. He orders a plane from Voisin, but when he flies it at Vincennes, it splits in two and crashes. Delagrange emerges unhurt (cf. Cronin 1991, 281).

Russian Second Duma meets for the first time; dissolved three months later by the Tsar. Bülow Bloc formed.
[February 2]:
Writes to Guillaume Apollinaire.
February 4: Documents Commentary
Sends a postcard to Gertrude Stein at No. 27, rue de Fleurus; tells her of Vollard's new agreement - to buy out his studio for 2,500 FRF, the balance to be paid in six months, 500 FRF more than he had paid the previous year: "Vollard came this morning. The deal is settled" (cf. Cousins & Daix 1989, 342; Baldassari 2007, 334; also Richardson 1991, 474; Richardson 1996, 17; Madeline 2008, 19; Cohen-Solal 2023, 80).

"Picasso liked to have money, there is no doubt about that, and he liked to keep it; but what sets him apart from most men in this respect is the fact that getting it did not fill him with elation. He found the whole business exhausting, particularly if it was accompanied by bargaining; but much more that that, he hated parting with his pictures. This was one of the very few things that stopped him working: the deep depression would not lift for days. He loved his pictures, and he loved painting them - could not conceive painting without love" (cf. O'Brian 1994, 143-144; also Roe 2015, 160).

"He stuffed the bank notes paid to him in a wallet until it became so crammed he did not dare leave it at home, but carried it about on his person in an inner pocket secured with a safety-pin. But affluence was bought at a price: he loathed parting with his own pictures. 'Picasso was always distraught at having to sell his paintings,' reports Fernande" (cf. Vallentin 1963, 81; also Unger 2018, 199).

"He was always distraught when he had to sell a painting. After the business had been concluded, the canvases taken away, he was despondent and wouldn't be able to work for several days. All this exhausted him: pressure from the buyer, the haggling, and the prolonged uncertainty. By the end he would be so fed up that, if it had been up to him and there was no one around to help him, he would have given it all away for nothing or thrown the dealer out the door just to be done with it" (cf. Olivier 1933, 144).

Apollinaire meets up with Géry Piéret, coming from Brussels, at the train station in Paris (cf. Richardson 1996, 20). He is a charming sociopath with a long trail of blackmail and larceny behind him. He had met the young Belgian on one of his late-night prowls of Paris' seedier districts (cf. Unger 2018, 310).

The trial for Stanford White's murder starts in New York. As a sixteen year old girl, model, actress and Gibson Girl Evelyn Nesbit had been debauched by prominent New York architect, Stanford White. On JUNE 25, 1906, White had paid for taking Evelyn's virginity when her new husband, the wild Pittsburgh millionaire Harry K. Thaw, had taken White's life on the rooftop garden of Madison Square Garden. The 1906 murder of Stanford White by Harry K. Thaw would quickly become known as "The Crime of the Century" and Evelyn Nesbit as "The Girl in the Red Velvet Swing." The shocking story and the lurid details which emerge from Thaw's trial become a modern morality tale for early Twentieth Century America. Nesbit, Thaw and White enact an archetypical tragedy of sex and violent death on a dark, urban stage. The story is a disturbing marriage of the breaking of ancient taboos and the anxiety of life in an ultimately unknowable city; a tale of innocence lost in a myriad of ways. Evelyn Nesbit is Fernande's "one ideal" (cf. Roe 2015, 214).
February 13:
Vollard gives him a down-payment of 1,400 FRF for a batch of canvases and drawings (cf. Rabinow 2006, 110; also Richardson 1996, 17; Kellein 2011, 129). (Some report the amount he receives as 1,500 FRF - cf. Geelhaar 1993, 17). (Others only mention the total as 2,500 FRF - cf. Daix 2007, 15).
Late-February:
Matisse is back in Paris; will remain until LATE-APRIL (cf. Cousins & Elderfield 1992, 136). (Others date his return to Paris to EARLY-MARCH - cf. Baldassari, Cowling, Laugier & Monod-Fontaine 2002, 363).

Now that the Steins are entertaining both the "Matisseites and the Picassoites" (as Gertrude Stein had divided them), Picasso can no longer keep out of Matisse's way. He, too, begins to visit him regularly, keeping a close eye on his rivaľ's emerging work and beginning a life-long competitive dialogue which they played out in their work (cf. Roe 2015, 176).

He and Matisse visit each other's studios once a week (cf. McGregor-Hastie 1988, 50) and respond to their respective work in progress - even if it merely represented a challenge to go one better. Gertrude Stein encourages their rivalry at her salon; her brother Michael and his wife Sarah became Matisse's leading patrons. Nevertheless, their friendship will last a lifetime. In 1907 they will even exchange paintings.
February 22: Commentary
Kahnweiler takes an apartment with his wife at Rue Théophile-Gautier 28 in Paris and rents a minimal gallery space at No. 28, rue Vignon from a Polish tailor for 200 FRF a month, "as discreet as himself, hung with grey velvet and holland cloth" (cf. Vallentin 1963, 81; Unger 2018, 350). It is barely sixteen square yards in size (cf. Franck 2001, 153). (Others date the establishment of the gallery simply to FEBRUARY - cf. Richardson 1996, 36; Fraquelli, Cowling, Silver, Vasseur & Bremner 2016, 161 -; or later to MAY - cf. Ernoult & Lassale 2019, 164).

"He constructed a territory that escaped the official functioning of the State (the country's top collector). But this territory also escaped the control exercised on contemporary art by the all-powerful Académie des Beaux-Arts" (cf. Cohen-Solal 2023, 204).
February 25:
Apollinaire writes: "Dined at Picasso's, saw his new painting - an even pink coloring on flesh, flowers, etc., women's heads simplified and similar, men's heads likewise." This reveals that Les demoiselles d'Avignon [OPP.07:001] in its current state has not yet emerged (cf. Daix 2007, 15).
End-February:
Through Uhde, Alfred Flechtheim meets Kahnweiler at the Café du Dôme. Flechtheim would have close business contacts with him, and Kahnweiler's brother Gustav would later become his partner.

"Unlike his friend and compatriot Wilhelm Uhde, Kahnweiler pursued the buying and selling of art as a business, using his background in finance to set up operations on a professional basis. He had a keen eye for the next new thing and would take risks for artists he believed in. But he also suspected that there was money to be made by dealing in the most radical art and was smart enough to figure out how to turn his passion to profit" (cf. Unger 2018, 350).
February 27:
Guillaume Apollinaire and Géry Piéret stop by the Bateau-Lavoir (cf. Unger 2018, 310). In a notebook, Guillaume Apollinaire writes: "Evening, dinner with Picasso, saw his new painting: even colors, pinks of flowers, of flesh, etc., women's heads similar and simple heads of men too. Wonderful language that no literature can express, for our words are already made. Alas". As Guillaume Apollinaire's words indicate, even this most modern of writers was at a loss to describe a new kind of painting that, at the time, was clearly unprecedented. It is likely that in his shorthand way, he is referring to several paintings, preparatory studies of heads - of both men and women - for Les demoiselles d'Avignon [OPP.07:001] (cf. Cousins & Seckel 1994, 147; also Richardson 1996, 20; Blier 2019, 59).

"At then time Picasso was still in thrall to the brute power of the Iberian sculptures he'd seen thee previous year in the Louvre. Though he was actually careful to conceal the sources of his inspiration, on this occasion he must have discussed his passion with his guests, a conversation that apparently inspires Piéret to attempt some grand gesture that would elicit admiring gasps from his new friends" (cf. Unger 2018, 311).
February 28:
Clemenceau addresses the Chamber of Deputies. To describe what he has conceived as the symbol of modernity in policing, necessary for suppressing illegal anarchists, the minister of the interior offers a rare instance of self-criticism: "Our system of repression is archaic, prehistoric ... What we need is a judicial police, a police designed for the regular pursuit of scoundrels" (cf. Cohen-Solal 2023, 133).
Early-March: Documents Commentary
Géry Piéret steals two Iberian statues and a plaster cast from the Louvre (cf. Richardson 1996, 22; Baldassari 2007, 342; also Vallentin 1963, 119).

With the focusing of his attention on Iberian statuary in the Louvre - the stimulus of Iberian pieces would be especially relevant to the first concept, or 'Iberian' state, of Les demoiselles d'Avignon [OPP.07:001] - Picasso buys one of two Iberian sculptures from Géry Piéret, Guillaume Apollinaire's secretary, without realizing that he has stolen them from the Louvre (cf. Cabanne 1979, 114; Cousins & Daix 1989, 342; Richardson 1996, 22; Torras 2002, 106; Daemgen 2005, 19). (Others date this transaction simply to MARCH - cf. Daix 2007, 16). Piéret also leaves the second head at the Bateau-Lavoir studio, although the artist had refused to buy it (cf. Mahler, Perdrisot & Lowery 2015, 53). (Some claim that Picasso bought both statues - cf. Fluegel 1980, 86; Franck 2001, 114 -; others claim that Piéret simply dropped off the two statues - cf. Daix 2007, 46). This fact will come to the surface in AUGUST 1911. Study of these sculptures is reflected in stylized, scroll-like ear and other features of Tête d'homme [OPP.07:009].

The African dance masks found in Leo Frobenius’s book Die Masken und Geheimbunde (1898) may have served - like other visual materials for Picasso - as provocative muses, sorceresses that pressed the artist to think anew about not only image-making but also the world of art (cf. Blier 2019, 113).

At Derain’s urging, Picasso visits the Musée d'Ethnographie du Trocadéro, where he has 'revelation' about the sculpture from the African continent and Oceania (cf. Richardson 1996, 25; Franck 2001, 96; Daemgen 2005, 19). (Others date the visit more generally to SPRING - cf. Baldassari, Cowling, Laugier & Monod-Fontaine 2002, 364; Roe 2015, 177 -; later to MAY - cf. Daix 2007, 19; Mahler, Perdrisot & Lowery 2015, 54 -; to MAY or JUNE - cf. Fluegel 1980, 87; Dagen 2009, 484 -; to JUNE - cf. Inglada 2008, 114; Perdrisot-Cassan & Mattiussi 2021, 394; Philippot & Dareau 2021, 153 -; to END-JUNE or EARLY-JULY - cf. Cabanne 1979, 116 -; more generally to JUNE or JULY - cf. Daix cited by Richardson 1996, 25; also Mahler, Perdrisot & Lowery 2015, 54 -; or even more generally to SUMMER - cf. Warncke & Walther 1991, 146; Torras 2002, 106). Although Derain and Matisse have already begun to collect it, Picasso has paid no attention to it until now.

"If he was not the first modern artist to "discover" tribal sculpture, Derain was the first to see its potential as a catalyst. However, he was too full of doubt to do much about it for another year. By urging Picasso to visit the Ethnographic Museum at the Trocadéro, he relinquished to him" (cf. Richardson 1996, 76).

"Derain stopped along the way, yet he was the first to have introduced what was to become Cubism" (cf. Cabanne 1979, 118).

"When I went to Trocadéro it was disgusting. A flea market. The smell. I was all alone. I wanted to leave. But I didn't go. I stayed. And I stayed. I realized it was very important: something was happening to me, right? The masks were not sculptures like the others. Not at all. They were magical things. And why not the Egyptians and Chaldeans? We hadn't noticed: primitives, not magic! The Negroes were ‘intercessors' - I've learned the French word since then. Against everything, against unknown, threatening spirits. I was still looking at the fetishes when I realized that me, too, I'm against everything. Me, too, think everything is unknown, is the enemy. Everything, but everything, not just details: women, children, animals, tobacco, toys! I understood what Negroes used their sculpture for. Why they carved like that, rather than another way. All the same, they were not cubists! Because cubism didn't exist. Surely some guys invented the models, and other guys imitated them—that's tradition, right? But all those fetishes were used for the same thing. They were weapons. To help people become independent, to no longer obey the spirits. Tools. If we give a form to spirits, we become independent. Spirits, the unconscious (not yet discussed much), emotion, it's all the same thing. I understood why I was a painter. All alone in this dreadful museum, with masks, redskin dolls, dusty manikins. The Demoiselles d'Avignon had to happen that very day, not at all because of the forms: but because it was my ﬁrst canvas of exorcism, that‘s why!" (Picasso, quoted by Malraux, 1974) (cf. also Gilot & Lake 1964, 248; Unger 2018, 329-330; Cohen-Solal 2023, 154).

Picasso's initial visit to the Trocadéro had been to examine the Medieval sculpture casts in plaster that were on exhibit in the Musée de sculpture comparée, housed in the wing opposite the Musée d’Ethnographie (cf. Blier 2019, 94).
March: Item Commentary
"Picasso had become a recluse, he had virtually forsaken painting for drawing and was busy filling sketchbooks in preparation for Les demoiselles d'Avignon [OPP.07:001]." (cf. Richardson 1996, 9).

Through APRIL, works on a series of drawings in Sketchbook 1063 related to 'Brothel scenes'.

"[Picasso] sought to find a way to conflate - in a quasi-mystical union - earthy, exotic reality with sublime, classical beauty; in the search for this conflation ..., Picasso actually did emulate the classical canons, in his own way, with the help of Albrecht Dürer" (cf. Lavin 2007, 61).

"The artist, who freely admitted sleeping with most of his models, was doubtless seeing other women ... Picasso may also have reverted to his old habit of frequenting brothels. Since his subjects usually reflect the circumstances of his daily life, this is more than likely. Citing Françoise Gilot's assertion that Picasso confessed to having caught and been cured of an unspecified venereal disease at some unspecified time before his first marriage, Rubin hazards a guess that this occurred in the course of this winter and that "trepidation in regard to syphilis and gonorrhea had to play some role in [the Demoiselles'] symbolism" (cf. Richardson 1996, 18).

Léon Delagrange flies a similar plane at Bagatelle as in FEBRUARY, but this time goes 85 meters. This is the first flight to be filmed - by Gaumont (cf. Cronin 1991, 281).
March ~ April: Item Commentary
Evolving conception of the brothel composition with seven figures - five nude women, a sailor seated in the middle, and a medical student at the left (perhaps holding a skull) as in Les demoiselles d'Avignon (Étude) [OPP.07:345] (cf. Fluegel 1980, 86).

Also paints the oils on canvas Les demoiselles d'Avignon: buste de femme (Étude) [OPP.07:015], Tête de femme, profil gauche [OPP.07:343]; the oils on board Tête de femme à la peinture rouge [OPP.07:344]; the gouache Les demoiselles d'Avignon: lhomme debout de profil, 'étudiant en médecine (Étude) [OPP.07:311]; the pastel Les demoiselles d'Avignon: profil d'homme, l'étudiant en médecine (Étude) [OPP.07:305]; the drawing in ink Feuille d'études pour l'étudiant en médecine [OPP.07:286].

"Whether or not Picasso was sleeping with other women, Fernande would have had reason to resent the demoiselles as bitterly as if they had been flesh-and-blood rivals. Had they not taken Picasso away from her?" (cf. Richardson 1996, 20).

A sketchbook of Picasso's, in which he executes primarily studies of one of the figures in the six-figure sketch for Les demoiselles d'Avignon [OPP.07:001], the woman with arms raised, bears, in Picasso's hand, on the inside front cover, the following inscription: "Eugène Rouart Bagnols-de-Grenade par St Jory Haute Garonne Adresse télégraphique Rouart-Capy-St-Jory;" and on the inside back cover: "Jueves a las 12 au restaurant Foyot Eugène Rouart" (cf. carnet No. 4; Seckel, 170, 175). The entry is directly related to the two letters from Eugène Rouart (cf. MARCH 30 and APRIL 27). The lunch, on a Thursday, may have taken place in MARCH (we know that Picasso and Rouart saw each other before the 30th); the APRIL 27 letter does not indicate whether they had seen each other again since MARCH 30. The final page of the same sketchbook bears the note: "Escribir à Braque / Stein estará en su casa / toda la semana proxima / menos el lunes y el martes." On the inside back cover: "Braque El viernes." On the inside front cover, along with Rouart's address, "Salle II" (cf. Carnet No. 4; Seckel, 170, 175). Picasso has to write to Braque. Are they supposed to meet on a Friday? Have they already made each other's acquaintance, and if so, where? The reference to "Stein" confirms the presence of either Leo or Gertrude in Paris at the time. Does "Salle II" refer to a room in the Salon des Indépendants (MARCH 20-APRIL 30)? (cf. Cousins & Seckel 1994, 149).

"Braque already knew Picasso by reputation since he had spent the SUMMER of 1905 in the company of two of his closest friends, the sculptor Manolo and the critic Maurice Raynal, who had traveled with him to his hometown of Le Havre. He was also acquainted with Apollinaire from Paulette Philippi's opium den on the rue de Douai (which Picasso and Fernande also attended on occasion). On the basis of Uhde's recommendation, Picasso had agreed to meet with the young painter, despite the fact that he had grown more reclusive after his return from Gósol" (cf. Unger 2018, 301).

At an unspecified date, possibly on the occasion of a studio visit during the period of the Salon des lndépendants, Braque leaves Picasso his calling card, on which he has written: "Anticipated memories!" (cf. Cousins & Daix 1989, 343; Richardson 1996, 68).

By this time, cinema is a weekly ritual for Picasso and his friends. "Each Friday la bande à Picasso eagerly trooped over to rue de Douai to see the latest motion picture. Especially at the time of Les demoiselles d'Avignon [OPP.07:001], the cinema is Picasso's other passion. With his flair for self-dramatization, he develops the menacing look of silent-screen actors that can be seen in contemporary photographic self-portraits, and his companion Fernande began to look "like a screen vamp." Cinema is very cheap, accessible to everybody, and located in Montmartre. They may have been attending the Omnia Cinema, which had opened in DECEMBER 1906 with a first-run program that changed every Friday. It was not far from Méliès's Robert-Houdin Theater and near the Place Pigalle on the Boulevard des Italians (cf. Rose 2007, 39).
